task.goal: Create a low-pressure way for a repair café to celebrate failed repair attempts as useful learning rather than shame.
hard_constraints: Four volunteers have a table, paper and a small display board for one monthly event.
No photos or names without explicit consent, no prizes or leaderboards, and no unsafe repair advice.
Participation is optional, usable without public speaking, and does not slow the queue substantially; pilot with observation and opt-out checks.
task.available_resources: Existing repair notes with permission to summarize anonymously.
task.expected_result: A concrete ritual and evaluation of learning versus embarrassment.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Useful Ending
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make an unsuccessful repair produce a small, optional learning record. The mechanism is to give the attempt a useful endpoint: an observation or boundary worth remembering, even when the item remains broken.

At handback, a volunteer offers a paper slip: “Still broken; now we know…” The owner can tick “one possibility ruled out,” “a limit identified,” “a question clarified,” or “nothing clear yet,” then optionally add a sentence. No explanation aloud is required. Blank slips are fine. The owner keeps the slip unless they separately consent to an anonymous summary appearing on the board. A volunteer reviews any shared wording, removing identifying details and procedural repair advice. The board heading reads “Useful endings this month.” Permitted existing notes can supply a few examples without implying that their owners joined this ritual.

Four volunteers use one table corner for slips and the small board for summaries. The handback volunteer makes the offer; another reviews contributions during quiet moments. Folding paper creates separate collection pockets for publication consent and private feedback. Participation should take under a minute away from the service queue.

This assumes some visitors value a concrete record of what changed. It may feel forced when nothing useful emerged, so “nothing clear yet” must remain an equally acceptable ending. The ritual celebrates careful inquiry without claiming every failure is beneficial.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate short handback periods offering either an ordinary repair summary or that summary plus the optional slip. In both periods, offer anonymous exit ticks: “I learned something useful: yes/unsure/no” and “The handback made me feel embarrassed or pressured: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes handback time and whether declined offers are accepted immediately, without recording identities. Inspect whether completed slips contain a specific observation rather than compulsory positivity. The idea is weakened if learning responses resemble the comparator while embarrassment, pressure, or delays increase. Low response numbers and self-selection limit conclusions; do not treat uptake as proof of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Open Questions Board
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Celebrate failed attempts by treating them as contributions to the café’s shared understanding of uncertainty. The mechanism is collective sense-making: an unresolved item can reveal a recurring question worth investigating, without putting its owner on display.

Before the event, volunteers turn permitted repair notes into three or four anonymous, non-procedural questions, such as “What information was missing before diagnosis?” or “When did we recognize that this repair exceeded our facilities?” Each card includes an honest statement of what remains unknown. Avoid item descriptions that could identify someone.

Visitors may silently read the board, place a pencil mark beside a question that helped them understand their own visit, or submit a new question on paper. Nothing requires describing their repair publicly. New submissions need a separate publication-consent tick and volunteer review. The closing ritual is a handwritten board footer: “These questions are worth carrying forward,” followed by one or two questions selected for relevance and safe scope, without vote totals or rankings. No promise of a future answer is made.

One volunteer prepares the initial cards, one checks proposed additions during quiet periods, and all four continue their ordinary repair roles. Reading and marking happen at the table edge after handback, outside the queue.

This assumes shared uncertainty can reduce isolation and support learning. It could instead resemble a catalogue of inadequacy or invite speculative technical advice. Keep all cards about observations, information needs, and service limits; omit repair instructions and unsupported explanations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Display the same permitted note summaries first as plain anonymous accounts and then as open questions, switching order midway through the event if practical. Offer separate optional paper responses: “What, if anything, did this help you understand?” and “Did this display make failed repairs feel more acceptable, unchanged, or more uncomfortable?” Observe congestion and whether visitors can bypass it easily. Compare the specificity of learning responses and reported discomfort between versions. The mechanism is doubtful if questions generate only vague approval, greater discomfort, or unsafe advice submissions. Different visitors and time periods make this a small design check, not causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Thank the Care, Leave the Outcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a private acknowledgment ritual to separate appreciation of a repair attempt from whether it succeeded. The mechanism is relational: a visitor can feel respected when someone recognizes a specific act of care, without having to reinterpret disappointment as success.

At handback, a volunteer may offer a folded paper card: “Would you like a short acknowledgment of the attempt? Passing is fine.” Inside, the volunteer writes one truthful, observable contribution, such as “You explained the fault clearly” or “We stopped when we reached the limits of our equipment.” Avoid praising persistence indiscriminately, assigning blame, or implying that stopping proves a repair was safe. The visitor can keep, decline, or discard it without explanation. There is no public reading.

A separate optional slip asks, “What care or effort would you like this café to recognize?” Visitors may acknowledge listening, patience, clear explanations, or respecting a decision to stop. With explicit permission, volunteers summarize these themes anonymously on the board under “Care we noticed today.” The board contains neither identifiable repair stories nor individual credits. This makes celebration visible while keeping personal acknowledgment private.

Four volunteers agree on a few factual wording examples before opening. Cards are completed only when handback allows; otherwise a visitor can take a blank reflection card to the table. One volunteer checks board contributions during a lull. Existing notes are unnecessary.

The approach assumes recognition feels supportive. It may seem patronizing, especially after a frustrating visit, and it does not itself establish technical learning. The offer must be brief, sincere, and easy to refuse.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare ordinary handbacks with handbacks offering the private acknowledgment during alternating short periods. Give both groups optional anonymous exit questions: “I felt respected,” “I can name something learned or a limit clarified,” and “I felt expected to be positive,” each with yes/unsure/no options. Observe added handback time, repeated offers after refusal, and any queue obstruction. A useful result would combine respect with identifiable learning or clearer limits, without increased pressure. Reject or revise the ritual if appreciation rises but pressure also rises, or if visitors describe it as patronizing. Sparse feedback leaves uncertainty; silence and acceptance are not evidence of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Volunteers Go First
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make volunteers’ own unsuccessful attempts visible before inviting any visitor contribution. The mechanism is norm-setting through example: when the people treated as experts acknowledge uncertainty and disappointment without self-mockery, visitors may feel less personally judged by an unsuccessful repair.

Before opening, each willing volunteer writes a short anonymous account of an attempt they personally made: “We hoped… / What happened… / What changed in our understanding…” Use only truthful accounts they consent to share. Include unresolved disappointment where appropriate; do not manufacture a lesson. Exclude identifying item details, repair instructions, and claims that an item is safe. Two accounts are enough if others prefer to pass.

Display these under “Our attempts sometimes end here too.” At handback, a volunteer can briefly point out that the board is optional reading, without asking the visitor to contribute or respond. Beside it, provide folded paper headed “Something I wish repair volunteers understood about an unsuccessful visit.” Visitors can deposit an anonymous private note without speaking. These notes remain private and are not added to the display.

During a quiet moment near closing, the four volunteers read the notes and write one collective acknowledgment on the board, such as “A disappointing outcome can still deserve a clear explanation.” This closes the ritual without displaying visitors’ experiences or requiring positive feelings.

The table, paper, and board suffice; preparation takes a few minutes, and reading happens beyond the queue. The approach assumes volunteer examples feel credible and relatable. It could instead undermine confidence or make visitors feel responsible for comforting volunteers. Keep accounts brief, avoid excuses, and never seek reassurance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot during one event with alternating display periods: a neutral description of the café’s repair limits versus the volunteer accounts. Offer the same optional anonymous exit slip in both periods: “An unsuccessful repair would make me feel judged here: yes/unsure/no”; “Something this helped me understand: ___”; and “I felt asked to reassure volunteers: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes queue obstruction and whether people can bypass the display and decline feedback without another invitation. Revise or stop if the accounts increase reported judgment, solicit comforting responses, or produce reassurance without identifiable learning. Different visitors, timing, and voluntary responses prevent a causal conclusion; uptake alone does not show comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Failed Attempt Changes Our Welcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give unsuccessful attempts a concrete consequence in how the café operates. The mechanism is visible institutional responsiveness: an attempt becomes useful because the café changes a small practice in response, rather than asking its owner to find a positive meaning in the outcome.

Before the event, volunteers review existing repair notes that may be summarized anonymously. Choose one recurring, well-supported communication problem associated with unsuccessful visits—for example, visitors not knowing which equipment the café lacks. Do not infer a recurring problem from a single ambiguous note. Agree on one modest change achievable with paper, such as placing a plain-language facilities notice at the table.

Put a two-part card on the display board: “Earlier unsuccessful attempts showed us…” and “Today we changed…” Describe the communication gap and actual change without identifying visitors, blaming anyone, or giving technical repair advice. Label it “An attempt that changed the café.” This is the celebratory act: publicly crediting unsuccessful work with improving the service, without naming its participants or suggesting their disappointment was necessary.

After handback, anyone may silently leave a private slip completing “One thing that would have made today clearer…” Submission is optional and separate from service. A publication-consent box permits an anonymous summary, but private feedback remains useful without that permission. During a lull, volunteers may implement one feasible clarification and update the board only after doing so. If nothing suitable emerges, leave the original change visible rather than inventing progress.

All four volunteers retain their repair roles; one checks slips during quiet periods. This requires authority to make small communication changes and enough permitted notes to identify a genuine issue. It cannot compensate for a poor repair explanation, and the board could feel promotional unless it states the change modestly and honestly.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For a small prototype, alternate between displaying the new facilities notice alone and displaying it with the anonymous account of why it changed. Keep the actual service improvement available throughout. Offer optional exit ticks: “I understand this café’s limits”; “Unsuccessful attempts seem useful to improving this café”; and “This framing made my disappointment feel dismissed,” each with yes/unsure/no, plus space for an example of something learned. Observe congestion, unobstructed opt-out, and whether volunteers pursue declined feedback. The proposed mechanism is weakened if the origin story adds no understanding or usefulness, or increases dismissal. Inspect whether the promised change actually happened. One event provides a practical design check, with substantial uncertainty from small numbers and self-selection.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Hindsight Fold
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Turn a permitted account of an unsuccessful repair into a silent, folded-paper exercise that lets visitors experience how uncertainty changes with information. The mechanism is perspective-taking: an outcome can look obvious afterward, while an honest reconstruction shows why the attempt was informative.

Before the event, two volunteers select one existing repair note with permission for anonymous summarization. It must document both an initial uncertainty and something the attempt actually established. If no note supports that sequence, do not manufacture one. Remove identifying details and all procedural repair advice.

The outside of a folded sheet gives the initial situation in broad terms and asks: “Could you tell whether a repair would be possible from this information?” Readers can privately consider “yes,” “no,” or “unsure,” without submitting an answer. Inside, reveal the documented outcome and the specific information gained. Include “The item remained unrepaired” plainly. The final line reads: “This attempt gave us a case worth learning from. Disappointment can remain.” There is no correct-answer score, public response, or invitation to diagnose the item.

Place a few copies at the table edge, clear of the queue. The board holds the same folded case under “An unsuccessful attempt, a useful lesson.” Opening the fold is the optional ritual; visitors need neither speak nor contribute their own experience. Two volunteers prepare and check the wording before opening; all four retain their ordinary roles during service.

This assumes the notes preserve enough information to reconstruct uncertainty faithfully. A selective account could excuse poor work or exaggerate learning. Use modest claims and omit cases whose educational value depends on technical instructions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate the folded version with an unfolded version containing exactly the same account. Offer optional anonymous slips asking: “What did this attempt establish?”, “Did this make unsuccessful repairs feel less shameful, unchanged, or more shameful?”, and “Did you feel tested or pressured?” Observe obstruction and whether visitors can ignore the display without prompting. Stop or revise if the fold attracts guessing but yields no clearer learning, increases embarrassment, or delays service. Sparse, self-selected feedback cannot establish effectiveness; inspect unanswered and critical responses alongside favorable ones.

EXPAND.title: Agree on Two Possible Wins
EXPAND.proposal:
Make learning an agreed purpose before repair begins, so an unsuccessful outcome does not require a retrospective positive spin. The mechanism is expectation setting: visitors can choose whether clarifying uncertainty counts as a worthwhile outcome before knowing whether their item can be fixed.

At the table edge, an optional paper card says: “We hope to repair it. If we cannot, would you also value understanding what remains uncertain?” Choices are “yes,” “repair only,” and “skip.” No explanation is required. Taking a card does not change queue priority or the repair service.

For visitors choosing yes, the volunteer circles one realistic information goal during the ordinary intake: understanding the reported problem, establishing what information is missing, or explaining the café’s limits. At handback, the volunteer marks “clarified” or “still unresolved,” with one factual sentence if available. Neither result implies that the item is safe. The owner keeps the card; nothing is published. A fixed board message supplies the celebration: “A clearer understanding is a contribution, even when an item leaves unrepaired.” It contains no visitor records.

One volunteer prepares cards and the board; all four use the same brief intake wording. This assumes intake already includes a short conversation and that some visitors value an information goal. It cannot manufacture learning when diagnosis reveals little. If choosing a goal requires extra discussion, offer the generic uncertainty goal or skip the ritual.

Unlike “A Useful Ending,” this changes the agreement before the outcome rather than asking visitors to find value afterward. Its main risk is lowering expectations or making the café sound unwilling to repair.
EXPAND.experiment: For one event, the intake lead owns a small pilot comparing alternating periods of this approach with “A Useful Ending.” Use optional anonymous exit ticks for useful understanding, disappointment, and pressure to accept a failed outcome; invite one sentence identifying any learning. Another volunteer samples added intake time and checks that skipping receives no follow-up persuasion. Stop offering the cards if two observed intakes add over 30 seconds or anyone reports that participation affected service. Prefer the new route only if clearer learning or less embarrassment offsets its extra intake work. Small, different groups cannot establish causality.

EXPAND.title: The Volunteers Go First
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce shame by making experienced volunteers visibly own uncertainty. The mechanism is social modeling: an unsuccessful attempt becomes something competent helpers acknowledge about their own work, rather than a visitor’s story to disclose.

Before opening, invite each of the four volunteers to contribute an unsigned account of an attempt they personally made that did not succeed. Contributing is optional. Each account uses three sentences: “I expected…,” “The observation did not support that expectation…,” and “That changed how I understand….” Use only truthful recollections, omit customer details, and include no repair procedures or claims that an item was safe. A second volunteer checks wording. If nobody wishes to contribute, do not invent examples or borrow customer experiences as volunteer stories.

Display up to three accounts under “Even experienced repairers revise their thinking.” The monthly ritual is adding one dated, unsigned volunteer learning account before the event opens. Visitors can read silently or bypass the board. No visitor submission, speech, name, photograph, or public response is requested. Ordinary handback continues, including an honest explanation when nothing useful was established.

The table holds an optional private feedback slip and a folded-paper collection pocket. One volunteer owns preparation and removal of unsuitable text; the other volunteers retain their normal roles. The board must sit outside the queue’s walking path.

This assumes volunteers will share credible examples and that visitors see their own uncertainty as less discrediting when experienced people acknowledge it too. Unlike “Thank the Care, Leave the Outcome,” reassurance comes from a changed social comparison, not personal praise. The display could instead reduce confidence in the café, so examples must communicate honest revision without advertising competence or minimizing consequences.
EXPAND.experiment: The display owner alternates this board with a plain factual board saying that some repairs remain unresolved. At exit, offer anonymous ticks: “Failed repair feels less embarrassing / unchanged / more embarrassing” and “My confidence in the café increased / stayed the same / decreased,” plus an optional learning sentence. Observe obstruction and whether anyone appears to feel expected to read. Remove the display immediately if a contributor withdraws consent or a visitor identifies a supposedly anonymous case; suspend it after a report of pressure pending review. Compare reduced embarrassment and specific learning against preparation time and lost confidence. Reading or smiling alone does not demonstrate benefit.

EXPAND.title: A Failed Attempt Changes the Café
EXPAND.proposal:
Celebrate failed attempts through a visible improvement to the service. The mechanism is institutional responsiveness: learning has value because the café changes something it controls, rather than because a visitor accepts a more positive interpretation.

Before the event, two volunteers review existing notes that have permission for anonymous summarization. Identify one recurring, nontechnical obstacle within the café’s control—for example, visitors discovering only at handback that a missing accessory prevented assessment. Check that the notes actually support the pattern; do not infer a technical cause or blame the owner.

Choose one small, reversible service change that the four volunteers can sustain during the event, such as an earlier accessory check within ordinary intake. The board uses three short lines: “Earlier attempts revealed…,” “Today we changed…,” and “We will check whether it helps.” Omit distinctive item details and any repair advice. Add “Thank you to the attempts that helped us improve.” Publication must remain within the permission already granted for the notes; otherwise describe only the general service change.

At the event’s close, the owner adds “kept,” “revised,” or “not useful yet,” with an honest explanation. Visitors can inspect this silently, ignore it, or leave private feedback. Nobody must identify their own failed repair. If no supported, feasible improvement exists, do not manufacture one.

One volunteer owns the change, a second checks the source summary and board, and all four receive a short briefing. Unlike the Open Questions Board, this converts evidence into an observable organizational response. It assumes the café has a controllable obstacle; its limit is that a service improvement may prevent frustration without teaching visitors much about failed repair itself.
EXPAND.experiment: Pilot only one change for one event. Compare it with the café’s ordinary process during comparable short periods where switching is practical; otherwise treat the check as descriptive. The owner tallies the targeted obstacle without identities and samples queue delay. Optional feedback asks what the board helped visitors understand and whether it felt blaming or reassuring. Stop the change if it obstructs intake twice or creates confusion about whether an item has been assessed. Stop displaying any summary whose anonymity is questioned. Keep the ritual only if visitors can identify the lesson or targeted friction decreases without increased embarrassment or workload that the team cannot sustain. Board approval alone is insufficient.

EXPAND.title: Reveal the Outcome Last
EXPAND.proposal:
Help visitors experience how uncertain an apparently straightforward repair can be. The mechanism is correcting hindsight bias: seeing what was known before the outcome can weaken the assumption that an unsuccessful attempt should have been obvious or reflects someone’s incompetence.

Using permitted existing notes, two volunteers prepare two short anonymous cases with similar initial information but different documented outcomes. Only use cases whose records support both the starting information and the outcome. Remove identifying detail and all procedures. If suitable records are unavailable, this route is not ready to run.

Each folded paper card first shows a broad situation and asks, “From this information alone, can we know whether the café will repair it?” The inside reveals the recorded outcome and what additional observation changed understanding. It explicitly says that a café outcome does not establish whether an item is safe to use. The pair should demonstrate that similar starting descriptions can conceal different situations; avoid implying that every outcome is unpredictable.

Visitors may silently open either card at the table edge, without submitting an answer. The small board reads: “We celebrate finding out, including when the answer disappoints.” The monthly ritual is unveiling one evidence-backed pair. No visitor story or public performance is required. A volunteer checks the paper cards during quiet periods and removes speculative annotations.

Unlike the Open Questions Board, the learning comes from experiencing the gap between initial information and known outcome, rather than collecting unresolved questions. This assumes readable case records and visitors willing to spend roughly a minute. It could feel like a quiz or an excuse for poor diagnosis; use an invitation to explore, without right-answer scoring or claims about volunteer competence.
EXPAND.experiment: The board owner alternates the folded pair with the same case summaries displayed fully open. Offer optional anonymous feedback: “What could be known at the start?” and “Did this make failed attempts feel more understandable, unchanged, or more embarrassing?” Also ask whether it felt like a test. Compare specific recognition of uncertainty against reading burden and discomfort. Remove the invitation if visitors report feeling tested or the table obstructs the queue; revise any misleading case immediately. Retain the folded format only if it improves understanding over the simpler open summaries without added embarrassment. This checks interpretation of these examples, not improved repair judgment.

EXPAND.title: A Useful Ending, Checked Before Sharing
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “A Useful Ending.” Preserve its optional private learning slip, “nothing clear yet” option, separate publication consent, and reviewed anonymous board summaries. Change one consequential step: the repair volunteer must confirm any café-authored claim before it becomes a learning record. An unsuccessful repair does not itself establish that a possible cause was ruled out.

At ordinary handback, offer: “Would you like a note of what we established? Passing is fine.” Using the existing repair notes, the repair volunteer writes one supported observation, information gap, or café limit. If the evidence does not support a conclusion, write “We did not establish the cause today.” The visitor may add a personal reflection, clearly separated from the café’s finding. No procedures or assurances of safety appear.

The repair volunteer owns accuracy until the slip is handed back. If interrupted or unable to verify the finding within the ordinary handback, give the normal repair summary and offer a blank private reflection slip; do not create a verification queue or ask another volunteer to reconstruct the diagnosis. A second volunteer owns publication only after accepting an explicitly consented slip during a quiet moment. Unreviewed contributions stay off the board. The owner keeps the original; permission covers only the reviewed anonymous summary.

The board retains “Useful endings this month.” Four volunteers need only paper, the board, and their permitted notes. This assumes the notes or repairing volunteer can distinguish an observation from a hypothesis. Compared with the source, the added accuracy boundary reduces the risk of celebrating false learning, at the cost of fewer displayable stories. A disappointing or inconclusive ending remains acceptable.
EXPAND.experiment:
For one monthly event, one volunteer coordinates the pilot while everyone retains ordinary repair duties. Alternate short periods of ordinary handback and the checked-slip offer. Sample added handback time and observe whether refusals receive immediate acceptance, visitors can bypass the table, and interruptions trigger the blank-slip fallback.

Offer both periods optional anonymous exit ticks: “I learned something useful: yes/unsure/no” and “I felt embarrassed or pressured: yes/unsure/no,” plus an optional sentence naming the learning. During quiet moments, inspect whether café-authored findings are supported by the notes; do not collect identifying details. Stop the slip offer if two sampled handbacks add more than 30 seconds. Remove any unsupported board claim immediately and suspend publication until its review failure is resolved. Keep the procedure only if specific, supported learning is apparent without increased pressure or substantial delay. Small samples and voluntary feedback cannot establish superiority; uptake alone does not establish comfort.

EXPAND.title: Two Truths Can Leave Together
EXPAND.proposal:
Use permission to remain disappointed as the ritual’s main mechanism. Learning can be recognized without requiring the owner to feel pleased about the failed repair. This removes an assumed dependency in many celebration rituals: accepting a positive interpretation before participating.

At the table edge after ordinary handback, place optional folded paper cards. The outside says, “An unrepaired item can still be disappointing.” Inside are two independent prompts: “How this feels, if you want to say” and “Something understood—or still unknown.” Either side may remain blank. Suggested feeling words include disappointed, relieved, frustrated, and no comment. The learning side accepts “nothing clear yet.” Visitors keep the card; nobody collects, reads, or displays its contents.

The small board supplies the shared monthly ritual: “We make room for disappointment. We appreciate careful attempts and honest learning.” Beneath it, display one short, non-procedural observation from existing notes already permitted for anonymous summary, explicitly labeled as a past example. Use it only if the record supports an actual observation or limit and can be summarized without identifying anyone. Otherwise omit the example and retain the invitation. The board celebrates inquiry without making anyone’s emotional response public.

One volunteer prepares the cards, another checks the example, and the other two continue their usual roles; no dedicated host is needed. Volunteers mention the table only once, if handback allows, and never invite a visitor to justify a feeling or extract a lesson. No names, photographs, repair instructions, prizes, or rankings are used.

Compared with a learning-only slip, the intended benefit is less pressure to turn disappointment into gratitude. The shifted risk is that explicit feeling language could make a routine visit feel intrusive or amplify frustration. It assumes visitors find private acknowledgment useful; the card cannot create technical learning that the repair did not produce.
EXPAND.experiment:
At one event, the preparation owner alternates short periods with the two-prompt cards and a simpler learning-only card, keeping the same optional placement and factual example. Provide a separate anonymous feedback slip asking: “Could you leave disappointed without feeling judged?”, “Did you understand anything useful?”, and “Did this feel intrusive or embarrassing?” Include unsure and skip options, plus an optional learning sentence.

Observe whether people can ignore the table, whether volunteers pursue declined offers, and whether reading blocks the queue. Stop verbal invitations after any report of pressure or an observed repeated offer after refusal; remove the cards if the table repeatedly obstructs passage or feedback identifies the feeling prompt as intrusive. Continue ordinary handback in either case. Compare specific learning and embarrassment with the simpler card, including preparation and reading burden. Retain the extra emotional prompt only if feedback suggests it reduces pressure without obscuring learning. Sparse responses leave the mechanism uncertain, and private cards should never be inspected to compensate.
